newsitem.title: FINLAND: Russia says it won't change mind on NATO expansion.
newsitem.headline: Russia says it won't change mind on NATO expansion.

text.p: Russia said on Wednesday it would not drop its opposition to NATO enlargement but, on the eve of a U.S.-Russian summit, took a more conciliatory line on developing relations with its former Cold War foe.

NATO's plans to take in new members from Central and Eastern Europe will top the agenda when Russian President Boris Yeltsin and U.S. President Bill Clinton meet in the Finnish capital on Thursday and Friday.
"Russia's approach to NATO expansion will not change regardless of any summits, bilateral meetings and negotiations," Yeltsin's spokesman, Sergei Yastrzhembsky, told reporters.

In Helsinki a day early to open the Russian media centre, Yastrzhembsky said in a brief speech that the summit offered the chance to "lay down an outline for Russian-American partnership in the 21st century".
But he took a stronger line afterwards with reporters. Moscow understood NATO would go ahead with enlargement and wanted a relationship with the alliance, Yastrzhembsky said.
"But that doesn't mean that anyone can deny Russia the right to defend its point of view on this process up to the last minute, to the moment when the decision is taken," he said.
"From our side we will, up to the last minute, insist on our right to a negative approach to this plan."

At a Madrid summit in July, the 16-nation alliance will invite some former Soviet bloc states to start membership talks, probably Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic. Russia says it will be isolated and feel threatened as a result.
With both sides setting out their positions ahead of the summit, Yastrzhembsky's comments mirrored the tough approach taken by U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright on Tuesday.
She said NATO enlargement would go ahead with or without Russia's approval and that Moscow would not be allowed to prevent more countries joining in future.
But the presidential spokesman had words of praise for NATO's efforts to reassure Russia and meet its security concerns. The alliance is trying to work out a new charter on relations with Russia.
"Here a compromise is possible," Yastrzhembsky said.

"There have been some steps which show that NATO is more and more aware of Russia's real concerns...This is already a real step towards compromise. NATO is showing more realism in its negotiating position with Russia."

He was referring to recent statements from NATO that it sees no need to station nuclear weapons or foreign troops on the soil of new member states. Russia has sought such assurances but wants even stronger, binding commitments.
